newsitem.title: INDIA: India's army short of officers, chief says.
newsitem.headline: India's army short of officers, chief says.

text.p: India's army chief on Thursday said his force was short of young officers and said authorities had launched a campaign to draw more recruits.
General Shankar Roy Chowdhury told reporters in this north Indian city that his army of about 980,000 men was short of about 12,000 officers -- about 20 percent of total officer strength.

"This is not a problem of the army alone, it is a national problem and needs to be tackled in that spirit. Nevertheless we are taking various measures to promote the defence services in general and army in particular, so that more and more young men come forward to take it up as a career."
Authorities said last month members of India's armed forces will get hefty pay hikes that go beyond the recommendations of a government pay commission.

The government is expected to incur an additional annual financial burden of 61.2 billion rupees ($1.7 billion) on account of the hikes which would benefit around 1.4 million personnel in the army, navy and air force, they said.

Prime Minister Inder Kumar Gujral's government moved in to please disgruntled soldiers after the army chief led complaints from defence personnel that the recommendations of the Fifth Central Pay Commission fell short of their expectations.
The pay hikes would be implemented with retrospective effect from January 1, 1996.

India's Finance Minister P.Chidambaram, taking into account an anticipated hike in the wage bill, announced that the defence expenditure for 1997/98 (April-March) would be around 356 billion rupees ($10 billion), up from 295 billion in 1996/97.
Cadets starting out on a military officer's career will henceforth get 15,000 rupees ($420) a month, almost double the 8,000 rupees they were getting under the old pay scales.

Roy Chowdhury said he felt the need to draw more young men into short-service commissions which oblige five years of service "which they will find just great; and even if they choose to step out, they would still have learnt enough to qualify for the best jobs in the corporate world outside".
Roy Chowdhury retires on September 30 and will be succeeded by Lieutenant-General Ved Prakash Malik.
India's army has fought four wars, three of them with neighbour and arch-rival Pakistan.
"The security environment in the country requires us to be alert," Roy Chowdhury said. "The nation's security is affected by problems in Jammu and Kashmir and the Northeast."

Moslem separatists have waged a seven-year campaign for independence in the northern Himalayan territory of Kashmir, one-third of which is controlled by Pakistan. In India's north-east, tribal militants in Nagaland, Manipur and Assam carry on low-intensity guerrilla warfare.

Roy Chowdhury rejected charges of human rights violations in Kashmir and the north-east. Hospitals and local authorities say at least 20,000 people, including hundreds of soldiers, have died in Kashmir's violence.

"Let me make it clear to you that the term 'human rights' is not new for the Indian army; we have been practising it for generations and do not require anybody to teach us what it means," Roy Chowdhury said.

"This was explicitly spelled out in our 'rules for aid to civil authorities' that firmly laid down the principle of use of minimum force, good faith and impartiality; and let me tell you that these are being followed by our men under very very difficult circumstances," he added. ($1 = 35.7 rupees)
